title: Invariants
objective: Name what stays true on every pass of a loop, and use it to prove the loop gives the right answer.

sources.title: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed. (MIT Press, 2022): loop invariants (initialization, maintenance, termination)

simplifies: Here the invariant is checked by running the code on one list. A real proof argues it for any list: true at the start, kept true by each pass, and at the end it says exactly what we wanted.

quiz.prompt: For an invariant to prove a loop correct, which three things must you show?

options.text: It's true before the loop, each pass keeps it true, and at the end it gives the result you want
options.explanation: Right. Initialization, maintenance and termination: together they prove the loop works for every input.

options.text: The loop is short, fast and uses one variable
options.explanation: Those are nice, but they don't prove the answer is right.

options.text: It's true on the last pass only
options.explanation: Only checking the end skips the reason it's true. You need start, every pass, and end.

quiz.prompt: In this loop, what goes wrong if line 5 adds nums[i] twice?

options.text: Nothing: the total is still a sum
options.explanation: The invariant breaks: after the pass, total would be more than sum(nums[:i + 1]).

options.text: The invariant fails at the very next check, which pinpoints the bug
options.explanation: Right. A broken invariant tells you which pass went wrong, not just that the final answer is off.
Every check after that first pass would be wrong too.
